items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: one of the stars was a comedian known as Dusty Fletcher whom I had seen many times.

ctx.x: George Duvivier and Smittie had been friends for many years and Smittie told me that he was the first one to give George lessons in harmony. George was not a drinking person, so he did not have the same thing there in common as did Smittie and I. And speaking of drinking, Lyman Vunk could drink us all under the table and walk a straight line from Central Park to Times Square. He and Lamar had their bottles and a glass on the bandstand quite often. Lamar or Limmie as some people called him was not a heavy drinker,…

We had a show to play twice a night, The first one at 10:30, and the other at 1:30 a.m. There were chorus girls, singers and the usual cabaret routine, but one of the stars was a comedian known as Dusty Fletcher whom I had seen many times. But the act that he did was very funny and sometimes, above the heads of some of the clients, because it was typical Negro comedy, and the Broadway cabaret cliental were mostly well-to-do white people. Dusty proved one thing in his act, and that was the statement many white…

The highlight of Dusty's act is when he arrives home drunk and has no key. He rooms with a friend named Richard, and they are both so poor that they only have one suit of clothes between them. When one goes out, the other has to stay home. When Dusty discovers that he has no key, he calls out, 'Open the door, Richard'. There is no response, and then Dusty says, 'I know he hasn't gone out, because I've got on the clothes,' after which he starts to climb up a ladder, singing "Open the door, Richard". Where did he…
